articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Tuesday welcomed the Shiromani Akali Dal's (SAD) return to the National Democratic Alliance (NDA), as the BJP
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Tuesday welcomed the Shiromani Akali Dal's (SAD) return to the National Democratic Alliance (NDA), as the BJP and its former ally announced a tie-up for the upcoming Punjab assembly elections. PM Modi described the partnership as a "natural alliance" and said it would work towards Punjab's development and the welfare of its people. The reunion ends a six-year break in their alliance."Putting Punjab and the welfare of Punjabis first! I am extremely delighted that the Shiromani Akali Dal returns to the NDA family and that too on the Parkash Purab of Sri Guru Nanak Dev Ji," PM Modi said in a post on X."Ours is a natural alliance that will ensure Punjab gets pro-people governance that takes the state to new heights of progress. Nurtured by Atal Ji, Advani Ji and Sardar Parkash Singh Badal Ji, the Akali Dal-BJP Alliance has stood the test of time. I am confident that our Alliance will emerge as the preferred choice of the people of Punjab," he added.The BJP and SAD announced their alliance at a press conference, with Union home minister Amit Shah confirming that the two parties would contest all 117 assembly seats in Punjab.Shah said the chief minister's post would go to the SAD, which would be the "big brother" in the alliance. He added that the two parties would finalise a detailed manifesto soon.Shah said the alliance would focus on eliminating the drug menace, addressing farmers' concerns and promoting Hindu-Sikh unity."The BJP's promise of resolving farmer issues and promoting Hindu-Sikh unity will get a boost with SAD joining hands with us," he said.Also read: 'NDA is now complete,' BJP welcomes back 'oldest ally' Akali Dal ahead of Punjab pollsSAD chief Sukhbir Singh Badal described the tie-up as an "emotional alliance" and said the parties would work to resolve Punjab's issues, including drug abuse.Badal expressed confidence that the alliance would win more than 100 seats and predicted that the Aam Aadmi Party's tally would fall to single digits.BJP president Nitin Nabin said the partnership was a natural alliance aimed at the benefit of Punjab's people and the state's development. He said seat-sharing discussions would take place soon.The reunion comes six years after the SAD ended its 24-year alliance with the BJP in September 2020 over the Centre's three farm laws. The party withdrew from the NDA amid widespread protests by farmers against the legislation. The laws were subsequently repealed.SAD leader and then Union minister Harsimrat Kaur Badal also resigned from the Modi government.Shah said the farm laws had since been withdrawn and there was no reason for them to become an issue in the renewed alliance.Speculation about a reunion gained momentum after Sukhbir Singh Badal met Modi at Parliament House in August. Shah subsequently predicted an NDA government in Punjab during his recent visits and public remarks.Elections to the 117-member Punjab assembly are due early next year.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: India's health bill: Who really pays?
articles.summary: Explore how the Ayushman Bharat initiative is reshaping India's healthcare landscape, revealing key insights into government spending versus household payments and the implications for citizens' financial health.
articles.body: In October 2026, a 27-year-old woman from Mathura who had lost the ability to walk underwent two complex spinal operations in Lucknow. At a private hospital, doctors estimated, the treatment could have cost Rs 6–7 lakh. Under Ayushman Bharat, she received it free, TOI reported.That same month, in Odisha's Bargarh district, a daily-wage worker was borrowing money to buy medicines for his family. His son's chemotherapy was covered under Ayushman Bharat, but as TOI reported, the family's monthly medicine requirements alone amounted to Rs 20,000.Both stories point to the same reality, albeit with different outcomes. The government is now picking up a larger share of the country's health bill, yet on the ground, massive medical costs can still push individual households into financial distress.Imagine India's entire healthcare bill as Rs 100. In 2013–14, families paid Rs 64.20 directly from their pockets, the government spent Rs 28.60, and other sources financed the remaining Rs 7.20.By 2023–24, the government's share had risen to Rs 43.50, while direct household payments accounted for Rs 42.70. Other financing arrangements, including private insurance, accounted for the remaining Rs 13.80. In absolute terms, government health expenditure rose from Rs 1.30 lakh crore in 2013–14 to Rs 4.14 lakh crore in 2023–24. Direct household payments increased much more slowly, from Rs 2.91 lakh crore to Rs 4.06 lakh crore. Government spending thus exceeded direct household payments by around Rs 8,000 crore.Government expenditure first overtook direct household payments in the National Health Accounts series in 2021–22, when pandemic-related spending pushed its share to 48%. A closer look at the latest National Health Accounts reveals what lies behind these numbers.The hospital-building spendOf the Rs 4.14 lakh crore spent by the government in 2023–24, approximately Rs 1.13 lakh crore was capital expenditure on healthcare infrastructure, equipment and other long-term investments. Excluding that, government spending on current healthcare, which is the money used to provide services and goods during the year, stood at about Rs 3.01 lakh crore. Households, meanwhile, paid Rs 4.06 lakh crore directly.For every Rs 100 spent on current healthcare services and goods, the government accounted for Rs 36, while households paid Rs 48.50 directly. Other sources financed the remaining Rs 15.50.However, government spending on current healthcare also more than tripled, from about Rs 98,000 crore in 2013–14 to Rs 3.01 lakh crore in 2023–24. The government's share of current healthcare expenditure rose from 23.2% to 36%.Nearly half the decade-long decline in the household share of total healthcare spending occurred in a single year, when it fell from 58.7% to 48.8% in 2017–18. This coincided with a change in the survey used to estimate household health expenditure and preceded the September 2018 launch of PM-JAY. How much of the decline was attributable to the change in estimation remains unclear.What changed over the decade?Government health expenditure increased by approximately 219% over the decade, without adjusting for inflation. Direct household payments grew by about 40%. For every Rs 100 the government spent on health in 2013–14, it was spending about Rs 319 a decade later. For households, Rs 100 became about Rs 140.Ayushman Bharat, launched in 2018, has been a prominent initiative in this expansion. Its hospital insurance component, the Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana (PM-JAY), provides eligible families with annual health cover of up to Rs 5 lakh for specified hospital treatments. In October 2024, eligibility was extended to all senior citizens aged 70 and above, irrespective of their economic status. But India's increased public spending goes well beyond hospital insurance.Government-financed health insurance schemes, including PM-JAY and state-specific schemes, accounted for Rs 33,385 crore in 2023–24, or about 8% of government health expenditure. A much larger part of public spending supports the healthcare system itself. Government spending on primary healthcare, the first point of contact for many patients, increased from about Rs 50,000 crore in 2013–14 to Rs 1.53 lakh crore in 2023–24. It accounted for roughly half of the government's current health expenditure in 2023–24.Through the National Health Mission and Ayushman Arogya Mandirs, the government has sought to expand basic consultations, maternal and childcare services, access to essential medicines and diagnostic tests. State and local governments accounted for nearly 68% of government health expenditure in 2023–24, underscoring their role in this expansion.One country, very different health billsIn 2023–24, government expenditure exceeded direct household payments in 13 of the 21 states and UTs for which the National Health Accounts provided comparable estimates. In the other eight, families still paid more directly. In Uttarakhand, the government accounted for 66% of total healthcare expenditure, whereas households paid 26.7% directly. The government's share stood at 57.9% in Odisha and 59.5% in Assam.Kerala shows the opposite pattern. For every Rs 100 spent on healthcare in the state, households contributed Rs 65.20 directly, against Rs 25 from the government. In West Bengal, the figures were Rs 63 and Rs 30. State-level government expenditure figures include spending by the Union government and local bodies, not merely the state government's own health budget. The estimates for household spending are based on survey data from 2017–18, updated for subsequent years.What happens when you walk into a hospital?The 2025 National Sample Survey indicated that health insurance or healthcare financing coverage has risen from fewer than one in five Indians in 2017–18 to nearly half, largely through government-sponsored schemes.At least half of outpatient treatment episodes at public facilities involved no direct medical expenditure. Average out-of-pocket medical expenditure per hospitalisation, excluding childbirth, was Rs 6,631 at public facilities against Rs 50,508 at private hospitals. While the types of treatment may differ, private hospitals, including those empanelled under government schemes, accounted for 60.3% of hospitalisations excluding childbirth.Medicines remain a major financial burden, with households spending Rs 1.71 lakh crore on separately purchased medicines in 2023–24, accounting for roughly 42% of their direct healthcare expenditure. While PM-JAY primarily covers hospitalisation, initiatives such as government free-drug programmes and Jan Aushadhi seek to reduce everyday medical costs. The number of Jan Aushadhi outlets rose from around 80 in 2014 to around 11,000 by March 2024.Who ultimately pays?Families also finance healthcare through insurance premiums. Expenditure through private health insurance, which includes employer-based group cover and individual policies, rose from 3.4% of total health expenditure in 2013–14 to 10.2% in 2023–24. When we look at where healthcare funds originate, including household insurance contributions, the picture changes. Households supplied Rs 55.70 of every Rs 100 spent on current healthcare in 2023–24, down from Rs 72.90 in 2013–14. The contribution from government budgets and grants rose from Rs 21.10 to Rs 34 over the same period.There is also a cost that the National Health Accounts cannot capture: the treatment someone needed but could not afford. A patient treated free at a government hospital and someone who forgoes treatment because it is unaffordable can both record zero direct medical expenditure. Their experiences could hardly be more different. The real measure of India's healthcare progress is whether an Indian can afford to fall ill without becoming poor.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: A Brooklyn woman discovers that her neighbour has attached a white fence to her house using screws and hardware while occupying a three-foot strip of her land; the court orders the fence removed as the neighbouring property goes up for sale
articles.summary: A Brooklyn homeowner has secured a court order against her neighbours after alleging that they attached a white fence directly to her house using screws
articles.body: A Brooklyn homeowner has secured a court order against her neighbours after alleging that they attached a white fence directly to her house using screws and other hardware while occupying a three-foot-wide strip of her property. Lorena Volokhova, who owns a house on Lake Avenue in Brooklyn, New York, claimed that the adjoining property owners had extended their occupation beyond their boundary and caused damage to her home's exterior. The dispute became more urgent when the neighbours began preparing to sell their property, allegedly including the contested strip in the sale. Volokhova approached the court seeking intervention, and on July 10, 2026, a judge granted a preliminary injunction directing the neighbours to remove the fence and stop occupying the disputed land.How a white fence became the centre of a property disputeThe case involves two adjoining properties at 14A and 15A Lake Avenue in Brooklyn. Volokhova owns the house at 14A, while Hanardi Corp. is the registered owner of the neighbouring property at 15A. Khanna Nazarova was named as an individual defendant and identified in the proceedings as the corporation's principal, owner, officer and/or authorised representative.According to Volokhova's complaint, the neighbours occupied a three-foot-wide strip of land between the two houses, which she maintained was part of her property. She also alleged that they attached a white fence to the exterior of her house using screws, fasteners and other hardware.Volokhova argued that the fence was not simply positioned along the boundary but was physically fixed to her building, effectively allowing the neighbours to exercise control over the disputed strip.Screws allegedly compromised the house's exterior protectionVolokhova told the court that attaching the fence to her house had created openings and penetrations in its exterior. She alleged that these damaged the building's waterproofing, weatherproofing and protective systems, leaving it vulnerable to water intrusion and further deterioration.She maintained that the longer the fence remained attached, the greater the potential damage to her property. Her complaint included claims involving trespass, encroachment, property boundaries, quiet title, permanent injunctive relief and property damage.Neighbouring property sale raises urgency of the disputeThe disagreement took on added significance when Hanardi Corp. and Nazarova were reportedly preparing to sell the property at 15A Lake Avenue. Volokhova feared that the three-foot strip would be included in the proposed sale, potentially creating further complications if a new owner acquired the adjoining property.She also raised concerns that photographs used on real estate listing websites could give prospective buyers the impression that the disputed strip and the fence attached to her house were part of the property being offered for sale.To support her claim, Volokhova submitted two property surveys, one dating from 2004 and another dated March 31, 2026. She argued that both showed the disputed strip fell within the boundaries of her property.Woman approaches court without a lawyerVolokhova filed the case without legal representation and sought an urgent order requiring the neighbours to detach and remove the fence. She also asked the court to recognise her ownership of the disputed strip and prevent the neighbouring property from being sold with the contested area included.The defendants did not file opposition to her application for a preliminary injunction. The court considered her application, supporting affidavits, property surveys and other submitted documents before deciding whether interim protection was necessary.Judge orders fence removed and disputed strip excluded from saleOn July 10, 2026, New York Supreme Court Justice Aaron D. Maslow, sitting in Kings County, granted Volokhova's application for a preliminary injunction in Volokhova v. Hanardi Corp., Index No. 608/2026.The judge found that the two surveys supported her claim that the fence and the occupied strip were on her property. The court also concluded that she had demonstrated a likelihood of success in the case, the possibility of irreparable harm and that the balance of equities favoured granting interim relief.The order directed Hanardi Corp. and Nazarova to remove the white fence attached to Volokhova's house and stop occupying the three-foot-wide strip. They were also required to remove any property they had placed there. In addition, advertisements for the sale of 15A Lake Avenue were prohibited from representing the disputed strip or the fence as part of the property being offered.The judge required Volokhova to deposit an undertaking of $2,500 with the County Clerk as security connected with the preliminary injunction.Final ownership and damages remain to be decidedThe July 10 order provided interim protection to Volokhova, but it did not conclude the entire legal dispute. The judge left the question of a final declaration of ownership, permanent relief and any compensation for property damage for a later determination.The court also noted that the defendants had not yet answered the amended complaint and that Volokhova had not sought a default judgment. The ruling therefore addressed the immediate encroachment and the proposed property sale while the underlying case remained unresolved.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Samajwadi Party (SP) president Akhilesh Yadav on Tuesday said his party was willing to make adjustments and accommodations to secure an
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Samajwadi Party (SP) president Akhilesh Yadav on Tuesday said his party was willing to make adjustments and accommodations to secure an alliance with the Congress for the 2027 Uttar Pradesh Assembly elections, as seat-sharing discussions between the two INDIA bloc partners continued for the second consecutive day in New Delhi.Akhilesh said senior leaders from both parties were engaged in negotiations aimed at ensuring electoral victory, but refrained from disclosing details of the proposed seat-sharing arrangement, saying several aspects were still under consideration."Regarding the ongoing discussions, our party's senior leaders, along with those entrusted by the party to handle these talks, are currently engaged in the process. What exactly is being discussed? How many seats are being agreed upon, and how many could the other party potentially win? These matters are under consideration, so it is difficult to say anything definitive right now. Alliances are formed with the sole objective of winning; the purpose of an alliance is victory," he said.Emphasising the need for a united effort against the BJP, Yadav said the SP was prepared to make compromises given the electoral challenge ahead."The Samajwadi Party is committed to making adjustments and accommodations because the battle ahead is significant. The goal is to win, and we must win, especially against a political 'machine' like the BJP, we have to prepare accordingly and make the right decisions," he added.Akhilesh Yadav questions ECI, raises concerns over EVMsAkhilesh also questioned the functioning of constitutional bodies and the Election Commission of India (ECI), alleging that concerns were being raised over the possible addition of votes and the maintenance of electronic voting machines (EVMs)."Constitutional bodies have a duty to act fairly, yet questions are being raised about this very body. It is now being suggested that the BJP is planning to add approximately 3 crore votes. Furthermore, regarding the warehouses where EVMs are stored, who are the engineers tasked by the ECI with maintaining these machines? We are told that the machines are being 'serviced,' but no one knows who these engineers actually are," he said.Ram Gopal Yadav says talks positive, agreement expected in two meetingsAfter Tuesday's meeting, SP general secretary Ram Gopal Yadav said the discussions had covered individual constituencies and described the negotiations as positive."Look, we have discussed every seat individually, and the discussions have been very positive. However, 403 seats are a very large number, aren't they? So, the discussions have not yet been completed. But you can rest assured that we will finalise everything in the next two meetings," he said.SP proposes 26 seats for CongressAhead of the meeting, Ram Gopal Yadav had confirmed that the SP proposed allocating 26 seats to the Congress, including two constituencies won by the party in the 2022 Assembly elections, four where it finished second and 20 where the SP secured between 60,000 and 70,000 votes, while the Congress received around 2,000 votes."We have proposed offering two seats that the Congress won in the 2022 Assembly elections. Additionally, there are four seats where the Congress finished in second place, and 20 other seats where the SP secured between 60,000 and 70,000 votes, while the Congress received only about 2,000 votes," he told reporters.Congress submits list of 130 priority seatsThe Congress had submitted a list of 130 priority constituencies to the SP leadership during the first round of discussions on Monday. SP leaders agreed to examine the list and continue negotiations.Both parties agreed to contest the Assembly elections together and indicated that the seat-sharing arrangement could be finalised within the next two to four days.Describing Monday's meeting as cordial, Uttar Pradesh Congress in-charge Rajendra Pal Gautam said the discussions lasted around 20 minutes, with both sides approaching the negotiations positively."We took just about 20 minutes to wrap up day one of the talks in which we discussed the number of seats (with SP). The SP panel members heard us and said they would get back after talking to their party chief Akhilesh Yadav ji," Gautam told PTI.He said both parties were committed to contesting together and would reach a mutually acceptable seat-sharing arrangement. Uttar Pradesh Congress Committee president Aradhana Misra-Mona also indicated that an agreement was likely within the next two to four days.Tuesday's meeting was held at the residence of senior Congress leader Pramod Tiwari. The Congress delegation included Gautam, Misra-Mona, working president Imran Masood and Congress Legislative Party leader Virendra Chaudhary.The SP delegation comprised Ram Gopal Yadav, state president Shyam Lal Pal, MP Rajiv Rai, Awadhesh Prasad and MP Iqra Hasan.Azam Khan says 'the bicycle will win'Meanwhile, SP leader Azam Khan said no one could stop him from contesting an election, expressing confidence in the party's election symbol."Who can stop me from contesting an election? My bicycle will contest the election; the bicycle will win... Samajwadis' focus is very narrow. They see nothing beyond the bicycle. These people don't even think about cars, helicopters, or airplanes..." he said.BJP's Sanjeev Balyan says party will counter 2024 perceptionBJP leader and former Union minister Sanjeev Balyan said his party would seek to counter the electoral perception created by the SP and Congress during the 2024 Lok Sabha elections and return to power in Uttar Pradesh for a third consecutive term."We are making efforts to ensure that the perception created during the 2024 elections does not succeed this time. We will take these issues (development and law and order) before the people. The BJP will form the government again," Balyan told PTI Videos during an interview in Muzaffarnagar.The former Muzaffarnagar MP also dismissed the Congress's electoral prospects in the state, saying the party did not have a significant support base in Uttar Pradesh.On the SP's PDA (Pichhda, Dalit, Alpsankhyak) outreach, Balyan questioned the changing definition of the acronym used by Akhilesh Yadav."Let Akhilesh Yadav first give a final definition of PDA, then we can respond. Sometimes one group is included in it, sometimes another. If there was any PDA during his government, it was limited to a particular section of the backward communities," he alleged.Balyan further claimed that the SP government had failed to ensure adequate representation for different backward communities and Dalits, despite the party's current emphasis on social justice and representation.Asked whether the SP-Congress alliance's strategy, including its outreach through panchayats, had contributed to the BJP's defeat in several western Uttar Pradesh constituencies in the 2024 Lok Sabha elections, Balyan said electoral outcomes could not be attributed to a single factor.The 403-member Uttar Pradesh Assembly is scheduled to go to polls in February-March next year. The BJP has been in power in the state since 2017, winning two consecutive Assembly elections.The SP and Congress contested the 2022 Assembly elections separately. However, the two parties joined hands as INDIA bloc partners for the 2024 Lok Sabha elections and jointly won 43 of Uttar Pradesh's 80 parliamentary seats.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.summary: An Israeli airstrike killed Naeem Abu Nahel, the head of Hamas' internal security apparatus in Gaza, in western Gaza City on Tuesday, Hamas sources said.
articles.body: An Israeli airstrike killed Naeem Abu Nahel, the head of Hamas' internal security apparatus in Gaza, in western Gaza City on Tuesday, Hamas sources said.Reuters reported that the Israeli military and the Shin Bet domestic security service confirmed carrying out a strike against a senior Hamas member in a joint statement but did not identify the individual. They said further details would be provided later.The killing comes amid a series of Israeli strikes targeting senior Hamas leaders and commanders in Gaza, despite the US-backed ceasefire that came into effect in October 2025.In a recent strike on November 15, Israel killed Samir Abu Younis, identified as the commander of Hamas' Rafah Brigade, in an airstrike in southern Gaza. Hamas and the Israeli military confirmed his death.Earlier in November, Israeli strikes also killed seven Palestinian militants, including Jamal Abu Saeed, whom the Israeli military identified as the head of operations in Hamas' military intelligence arm.Oxfam flags Gaza contaminationOxfam, an international humanitarian organisation, has warned that nearly three years of Israeli military operations have left Gaza facing a deepening environmental crisis, with more than 99% of the territory showing indicators of potential contamination.The report flags a dangerous mix of heavy metals, explosive residues, asbestos from destroyed buildings and other toxic contaminants released by bombardment and the destruction of infrastructure. Prolonged exposure could increase the risk of respiratory diseases, cancers, organ damage, birth defects and stillbirths, it warns.The report also paints a grim picture of Gaza's water and sanitation crisis. All six wastewater treatment plants are out of operation, leaving untreated sewage to seep into groundwater and flow into the Mediterranean Sea. Recent winter storms have further worsened the situation, spreading contaminated water through streets and displacement camps.The crisis is compounded by restrictions on the entry of essential equipment, including machinery and spare parts needed for rubble removal and humanitarian operations.Israel's restrictions on specialist testing equipment and technical experts have also prevented a full assessment of contamination risks.The UN Environment Programme estimates that the war has generated more than 61 million tonnes of debris across Gaza, around 15% of which could carry a high risk of hazardous contamination.You use AI every day. She died in 2022, after which her son Charles ascended to the throne.The family's primary residence is on the Windsor Castle estate, west of London. However, they use Anmer Hall as a country retreat for holidays and short breaks.The report came as William visited Prime Minister Andy Burnham at the British leader's office, 10 Downing Street, in London.The latest break-in follows a similar incident in 2024, when two masked burglars broke into Shaw Farm on the Windsor Castle estate. At the time, William, Catherine and their children were sleeping nearby at Adelaide Cottage in Home Park.In May, a man was arrested following an incident at Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor's residence on the Sandringham estate. Andrew, William's uncle, was stripped of his royal titles by his elder brother, King Charles, over his links to convicted US sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.William and his family receive round-the-clock armed security protection as working members of the British royal family.You use AI every day. articles.title: China investigates Shanghai Communist Party chief Chen Jining for corruption, 4th member of Politburo to be placed under probe since 2022
articles.summary: Chen Jining, the Communist Party chief of China's financial hub Shanghai and a member of the ruling party's powerful Politburo, has been placed under
articles.body: Chen Jining, the Communist Party chief of China's financial hub Shanghai and a member of the ruling party's powerful Politburo, has been placed under investigation on suspicion of corruption, according to state broadcaster CCTV. CCTV reported on November 24 that Chen was suspected of serious violations of discipline and law, a phrase commonly used by Chinese authorities to refer to corruption-related investigations.He is the fourth member of the ruling party’s elite decision-making body to be placed under investigation during its current term, which began in 2022, something that has not happened in decades, South China Morning Post reportedThe development marks a major setback for one of China's senior political figures, given Chen's position in the 24-member Politburo, the Communist Party's top decision-making body. Chen serves as secretary of the Shanghai Municipal Committee of the Communist Party. The position makes him the city's most senior political leader.The investigation comes amid China's continuing anti-corruption campaign under President Xi Jinping, which has targeted officials across the party, government and military. China has intensified its scrutiny of public officials as part of the campaign, with investigations frequently announced through state media and disciplinary authorities.According to reports, Chen’s last public appearance was last Thursday, when he inspected the state-owned enterprise China Cosco Shipping Corporation in Shanghai. Chen, 62, is the first sitting Shanghai chief placed under investigation since Chen Liangyu was removed from office in 2006.Chen is believed to have had an unusual rise through China's official ranks. An environmental scientist by training, he earned a doctorate from Imperial College London and rose through China's elite Tsinghua University to become its president. He entered government as China's environmental protection minister before becoming mayor of Beijing. He joined the Politburo in 2022 and was named party secretary of Shanghai, China's financial hub.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: An Ohio woman spent years paying to maintain a Colorado property held for her daughters while her former husband stayed unreachable in Mexico; an appeals court says he must reimburse $101,723.27 after the divorce dispute
articles.summary: An Ohio man must pay his ex-wife $101,723.27 after she spent years covering taxes, insurance, utility bills, and repairs for a Colorado house he was
articles.body: An Ohio man must pay his ex-wife $101,723.27 after she spent years covering taxes, insurance, utility bills, and repairs for a Colorado house he was supposed to maintain under their divorce deal. The Ohio Sixth District Court of Appeals overturned a lower court decision that had dropped a contempt ruling against Willard H. Sturt and lowered what he owed. In its 20 November 2026 ruling, the appeals court decided his ex-wife, Diane F. Sturt, had the right to get back the money she spent keeping the Minturn, Colorado, home in good shape.The fight was over a house held for the former couple and their two daughters. Diane told the court that Willard quit paying the home's bills in 2020 and became hard to reach while spending part of the year in Mexico. In its ruling in Sturt v. Sturt, the appeals court found that the original divorce deal put Willard in charge of all costs tied to the house. It also ruled that Diane did not need his okay before setting up needed repairs and paying overdue bills. The court figured that Willard owed her $101,723.27 for insurance, property taxes, utilities, and upkeep, and sent the issue of lawyer fees back to the lower court for another look.Divorce agreement placed property costs on WillardDiane and Willard Sturt got married on 12 June 1993 and divorced on 6 January 2015. They have two daughters, born in 1993 and 1996. As part of the divorce deal, the pair agreed to put the Colorado house into a permanent trust for their benefit, with their daughters set to inherit it, and both parents named as co-trustees. The divorce ruling also spelled out how the home's day-to-day costs would be split. According to the court's decision, Willard had to pay all costs tied to the house, including mortgage payments, property taxes, utilities, and upkeep. Diane had to pay him back each year for either half of the real costs or $5,000, whichever was less, once he showed her the bills, invoices, and canceled checks. The deal separately required the pair to split property insurance costs down the middle, with Diane setting up the insurance payments and Willard paying her back for half of the premiums. This setup became the heart of the fight after Diane said Willard quit meeting his money duties.Former wife struggled to contact himDiane filed a request asking the court to find Willard in contempt on 19 September 2023. She claimed he failed to pay property taxes, insurance bills, utilities, and repair costs, forcing her to cover them. At a hearing on 1 October 2024, Diane told a magistrate that Willard stopped paying the home's bills in late 2020. She said she wrote to him at his Ohio house and tried to reach him through his job, but never got a reply. She testified that some utilities were close to being shut off and that repairs were needed to keep the house from falling apart. According to the judgment, Diane said she paid the past-due bills and set up the needed work because she felt the house had to be protected, turning in invoices and other records proving what she spent. Diane told the court she visited the Colorado home about twice a year, where her daughter and son-in-law had lived for the past two to three years. Willard, on the other hand, had not visited the house since their daughter moved in, according to Diane's testimony.Willard disputed the repair costsWillard admitted during the hearing that he quit paying the home's bills, including property taxes since 2020 and his share of the insurance. He claimed Diane let their daughter move into the house without asking him, arguing that having someone live full-time in what had been a vacation home drove up running costs and wear and tear. He also questioned how much Diane spent on repairs and criticized the workers she hired. According to the court judgment, Willard said he wanted to do some of the work himself or hire people who helped build the house, though he admitted those original builders were no longer around in the area. He agreed that several parts of the house needed work, including the outside, deck, roof, and heating system, and admitted the deck railings had fallen off and the original fridge was over 20 years old. Willard insisted Diane should have talked to him before setting up the work, claiming he could have gotten some repairs done for less money. The court also heard that Willard had no phone and spent much of his time in Mexico. He admitted getting some letters from Diane, but said she could have reached him on his current wife's phone, even though he acknowledged his wife would not take calls from Diane because the two women did not get along.Lower court initially reduced the paymentAfter the October 2024 hearing, a magistrate found that Willard failed to live up to his duties under the divorce deal. The magistrate figured he owed Diane $40,171.50 for insurance, taxes, utilities, and upkeep, found him in contempt of court, and handed him a 30-day jail term, which he could skip by paying what he owed and the 2024 property taxes by 10 March 2025. The magistrate also granted Diane $5,000 for lawyer fees and $150 for court costs. Both sides fought the ruling. Willard claimed Diane had no right to set up repairs and ask for money back without getting his okay first, while Diane argued the magistrate lowballed her costs and should have counted extra repair, insurance, water, and internet bills. On 23 September 2025, the Lucas County Court of Common Pleas sided partly with Willard by taking the repair costs out of the contempt ruling, saying the divorce deal did not clearly allow Diane to set up repairs on her own and then ask to be paid back. The lower court also wiped out the lawyer fee award and cut the amount of money Willard had to pay, prompting Diane to take her appeal to Ohio's Sixth District Court of Appeals.Appeals court restores reimbursementIn its 20 November 2026 decision, the appeals court tossed out the lower court's logic. The judges said the divorce deal clearly put Willard in charge of all costs tied to the Colorado house, and nothing in it required Diane to get his okay before setting up needed upkeep. The court also noted that Willard admitted walking away from his money duties even though he knew repairs and other bills were due, deciding he had purposefully ignored the divorce ruling and that the facts backed up the original contempt finding. The appeals court also rejected the claim that Diane could not get paid back for repair work she set up herself, saying the deal did not let Willard shirk his duties while leaving the house open to unpaid bills and decay. The judges ultimately figured that Willard owed Diane $101,723.27, instead of the $40,171.50 granted by the magistrate. The updated total covered insurance, property taxes, water, internet, and upkeep, adjusted for Diane's own share of the bills, and put the repair costs back into the money terms Willard must pay to clear his contempt charge.Attorney fees sent back for reconsiderationThe appeals court also took another look at the decision to wipe out Diane's lawyer fee award. It pointed out that the lower court denied the fees partly because it had removed the repair costs from the contempt ruling, so overturning that choice meant the lawyer fee question had to be looked at again. The case was sent back to the trial court to weigh whether granting Diane lawyer fees and legal costs would be fair and decide if another hearing on the matter is needed. The Sixth District Court of Appeals agreed with all five of Diane's points of error and overturned the lower court's September 2025 ruling in its decision, listed as Sturt v. Sturt, 2026-Ohio-4621, which came out on 20 November 2026.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: ‘Sitting at the feet of the same BJP’: Bhagwant Mann attacks Sukhbir Badal over alliance
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Punjab chief minister Bhagwant Mann on Tuesday criticised the newly announced alliance between Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) and Shiromani Akali
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Punjab chief minister Bhagwant Mann on Tuesday criticised the newly announced alliance between Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) and Shiromani Akali Dal (SAD) for the 2027 Assembly elections, accusing SAD president Sukhbir Singh Badal of aligning with the same party he had previously criticised over its handling of farmers' issues.In a video statement shared by the Aam Aadmi Party (AAP), Mann alleged that the Badal family had initially supported the three farm laws introduced by the Centre in 2020 but changed its stand after the farmers' protest gained momentum and widespread support.Referring to the resignation of then Union Minister of Food Processing Industries Harsimrat Kaur Badal, Mann claimed the Akali Dal had realised that it would struggle to survive politically in Punjab if it continued to support the laws."The BJP and the Akali Dal have formed an alliance. I would like to remind you of what they say to each other, how these people try to make a fool of the public. They feel that people forget things after some time. At first, the entire Badal family kept speaking in favour of these 'black laws', saying, 'That's a very good law, a very good law. It is amazing; if it does amazing work, then with this, the agriculture of Punjab will become very prosperous.' When the farmers' movement reached its peak and started getting support from all over the world, they realised this would be a mistake and that it would be difficult to survive politically in Punjab," he said."So, Harsimrat resigned and started speaking against those laws, claiming, 'The BJP is anti-farmer, the BJP is anti-farmer, we have sacrificed, the BJP is anti-farmer.' But by then, people understood that they were still in talks with each other and were separating from each other just to put on a show for the public," he added.Harsimrat Kaur Badal resigned from the Union Cabinet in September 2020, before the Lok Sabha voted on the farm bills. Days after the Rajya Sabha cleared the final bill, Sukhbir Singh Badal announced the SAD's unanimous decision to withdraw from the National Democratic Alliance (NDA).Mann also accused the BJP of neglecting Punjab's interests, citing the state's tableau at national events on Republic Day and Independence Day."The same BJP says that the tableau that comes out on January 26 or August 15 will not be Punjab's tableau in Delhi. We got this work done by fighting with them," he said.Targeting Sukhbir Badal over his earlier criticism of the BJP, Mann alleged that the SAD president had accused the party of interfering in Sikh religious institutions with the help of the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS)."The same BJP about which Sukhbir Badal used to say that Sikh organisations are being taken over by the BJP with the help of the RSS, that the BJP has captured the committee of Hazur Sahib in Maharashtra and the committee of Patna Sahib. Today, sitting at the feet of that same BJP, you are making a political alliance," he said.Appealing to people to support the AAP government, Mann said, "Aam Aadmi Party is your own party. There is a party living in your hearts. I will come at your call, wherever you call me. We will come and raise our voice in favour of Punjab."BJP and SAD revive alliance after six-year breakMann's remarks came after BJP and SAD announced on Tuesday that they would contest the 2027 Punjab Assembly elections together, reviving their alliance after a six-year break. The two parties will jointly contest all 117 Assembly seats, with the SAD taking the lead in the arrangement."Big brother will be Akali Dal. We will contest all 117 seats. Bada bhai hi chief minister hota hai (The elder brother becomes the chief minister)," Union Home Minister Amit Shah said at a joint press conference attended by BJP president Nitin Nabin and Sukhbir Singh Badal."Naturally, the Shiromani Akali Dal (SAD) will play the role of the elder brother. The Akali Dal and the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) will contest together. Both parties will jointly contest all 117 seats, while the Akali Dal will be in the role of the elder brother," Shah added.The announcement, made on Gurpurab, marked the revival of ties between the two parties, which ended their partnership in 2020 after the SAD withdrew from the NDA over its opposition to the farm laws.Under their previous seat-sharing arrangement, the BJP contested 23 of Punjab's 117 Assembly seats, while the SAD fielded candidates in the remaining constituencies. The two parties had jointly governed the state for 10 years before losing the 2017 Assembly elections, when the Congress returned to power under Captain Amarinder Singh.In the 2022 Assembly elections, the AAP swept to power, while the BJP and SAD, which contested separately, were pushed to the margins.Meanwhile, the Punjab BJP on Monday announced its 16-member state election committee for the 2027 Assembly polls, with state president Kewal Singh Dhillon heading the panel.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Pig farmer sells £200,000 greenbelt land to travellers in 'revenge' against wealthy neighbours after four-year feud; more than a dozen caravans arrive at Hampshire village
articles.summary: A quiet village in Hampshire, England, has found itself at the centre of a bitter dispute after a former pig farmer sold his eight-acre greenbelt land to
articles.body: A quiet village in Hampshire, England, has found itself at the centre of a bitter dispute after a former pig farmer sold his eight-acre greenbelt land to a group of travellers. The sale, reportedly worth more than £200,000, has left several local residents upset after the land was covered in tarmac and more than a dozen mobile homes and caravans were brought onto the property.But behind the controversial sale is a four-year dispute involving a family, their neighbours and the local council. Pig farmer Matthew Silvester, 39, says he lost his farming business and had to leave the land after years of legal battles and complaints from neighbours. Some residents, however, believe his decision to sell the property to the travellers was an act of revenge.How a family farming dream turned into a disputeWhen Silvester bought eight acres of greenbelt land at Hares Farm in South Warnborough in 2022, he wanted to build a peaceful life with his family and run a small farming business. Along with his wife, Helen Freeman, 34, he started The Woodland Pig Co, selling pork to the local community.However, their plans ran into trouble after neighbours from the nearby Pickaxe Lane area complained to the council about the couple living in a log cabin on the property without residential permission. Some houses in the area are reportedly worth more than £5 million.The couple had permission to use the land for farming but not to live there permanently. This led to a long-running dispute with Hart District Council.Farmer claims council officers secretly watched his familySilvester has accused the council of secretly monitoring him, his wife and their young son after receiving complaints from neighbours.He told the Daily Mail that council officers watched the family at different times of the day and night. He also claimed that officers used a neighbour's garden and bathroom to record their movements."We were a small family farm selling pork to our local community. The council put an injunction on our land, and then, for months, it watched us. Officers stood in the dark in a neighbour's field and a neighbour's bathroom," he said.He also claimed that neighbours were asked to inform council officers whenever the family returned to the property.A tribunal later found that Hart District Council had unlawfully carried out covert surveillance of the family. The council has since changed its internal policy following the findings.'I would rather break the law than animals die': Farmer explains why he returned to the cabinSilvester said he often returned to the log cabin to look after the pigs, particularly the 35 breeding sows on the farm.According to him, the animals needed attention during labour because they could accidentally crush their piglets if they rolled over or stood up."I would often go back to the log cabin to go and look after the animals," he said.Explaining why he continued visiting the property despite the restrictions, he added: "If there was anything I could do to prevent deaths and losses on the farm, which cost us money, I was willing to take the risks. So my rule was: I would rather break the law than animals die."He also recalled an incident on June 8, 2023, when he stepped outside the cabin at around 5.45am and found two council officers standing near a fence on a neighbouring property. They were carrying cameras, notebooks and pens.The tribunal also found that council officers had recorded the family from a neighbouring property's en suite the previous night.Legal battle forces farmer to shut down his businessThe dispute eventually reached the High Court. In November 2024, after a three-day trial, Silvester and his wife were found in contempt of an injunction and given 12-month suspended sentences.They were also ordered to remove the log cabin, along with its electricity and water connections.The couple said these restrictions made it difficult to continue running their farm. The legal expenses also became too expensive for them to manage."We lost everything," Silvester told the Daily Mail.He said the family tried to continue the business for some time but eventually decided to sell their animals and shut down The Woodland Pig Co.The couple are now planning to appeal the ruling. After giving up the farm, they decided to travel and have since visited Southeast Asia.Why did the farmer sell his land to travellers?After deciding to sell the property, Silvester was approached through an intermediary by a group of travellers. They reportedly offered him more than £200,000 for the eight acres of land.He accepted the offer, and his decision has now become a major talking point in the village.Silvester admitted that he found the situation ironic, given that some neighbours had earlier objected to his small farming business."I just laughed to myself that the neighbours who couldn't have a pig farm next door to them or a quiet family would all of a sudden have some gypsies keeping their horses there or something," he said.For him, the sale marked the end of a difficult chapter. However, his former neighbours have a very different view of what happened.More than a dozen caravans arrive over August Bank HolidayThe situation reportedly took a dramatic turn over the August Bank Holiday weekend.At around 5.30pm on Friday, August 28, residents spotted several men wearing hoodies and balaclavas carrying out work on the land.The new leaseholders reportedly brought diggers and vans onto the property and covered the field with tarmac. More than a dozen mobile homes and caravans were then moved onto the site.Residents described the development as a land grab and raised concerns about an unauthorised traveller site being set up in their neighbourhood.There have been similar planning disputes in parts of the Home Counties, where greenbelt land is bought and later used for residential purposes without permission. In some cases, owners apply for planning permission after the development has already taken place.Neighbours accuse farmer of taking revengeSome residents believe Silvester deliberately sold the land to the travellers because of the way he and his family were treated during the dispute.One anonymous resident told the Daily Mail that the sale had caused great distress to people living nearby."I've never met him but if it gives him the satisfaction he needs, he has completely destroyed our lives, our sense of family, our mental health," the resident said.The resident also claimed that the development had caused panic and anxiety among elderly and vulnerable people in the area.Silvester, however, said he learnt about the extent of the development through the Daily Mail's reporting. He claimed he was unaware of how much work would be carried out on the land after the sale.He also pointed out that the neighbours could have continued living next to a small family farm instead of facing the current situation.What has the council said?Responding to the controversy, a Hart District Council spokesperson said the case related to events that took place three years ago.The council also said it had changed its internal policy following the tribunal's findings and would ensure that any future covert surveillance was carried out with the proper authorisation.What began as a dispute over a family's log cabin and pig farm has now turned into a much bigger controversy. While Silvester has moved on after shutting down his business, residents of South Warnborough are left dealing with the consequences of the land sale.The eight-acre property that was once meant to be a peaceful family farm has now become the centre of a bitter village dispute.You use AI every day. articles.title: China probes Shanghai party chief Chen Jining in Xi's anti-corruption purge
articles.summary: China's ruling Communist Party on Tuesday launched an investigation into Shanghai party secretary and Politburo member Chen Jining over suspected
articles.body: China's ruling Communist Party on Tuesday launched an investigation into Shanghai party secretary and Politburo member Chen Jining over suspected violations of party discipline.Chen is the latest senior official to come under scrutiny in President Xi Jinping's long-running anti-corruption campaign.According to state media, Chen is being investigated by the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection. The brief announcement, however, did not provide further details.Xi has pursued an anti-corruption campaign for more than a decade, carrying out purges on a scale not seen since the rule of Mao Zedong.“The takedown again shows that Xi Jinping’s anti-corruption campaign has no limits,” Mingda Qiu, a senior analyst at Eurasia Group, said in an emailed statement. “This is the fourth Politburo member to fall, and the fourth sitting member brought down in the current cycle. The pattern is unprecedented.”Other Politburo members purged include Gen. Zhang Youxia and He Weidong, both senior members of the Central Military Commission, which oversees China's armed forces, and Ma Xingrui, a provincial party secretary.The post of Shanghai party secretary has traditionally been seen as a stepping stone to China's top leadership. articles.title: Iraq moves to control Kurdish oilfields; Erbil calls the move ‘unacceptable’
articles.summary: Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi on Tuesday ordered federal authorities to take control of all border crossings in the semi-autonomous Kurdistan region.
articles.body: Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi on Tuesday ordered federal authorities to take control of all border crossings in the semi-autonomous Kurdistan region. He also directed the federal oil ministry to manage oilfields in several provinces, escalating tensions with Kurdish authorities.The orders come amid a crackdown on an alleged oil-smuggling network involving Iraq's state-run North Oil Company, according to Reuters.Zaidi also ordered the closure of unofficial border crossings and seasonal roads connecting the Kurdistan region with neighbouring provinces. He directed security forces to strengthen surveillance of oilfields and pipelines to prevent illegal oil trade.The prime minister further instructed the Kurdistan Regional Government (KRG) not to authorise crude oil or petroleum product exports without approval from the federal oil ministry.Kurdistan Region Prime Minister Masrour Barzani rejected Baghdad's decision, calling it unacceptable and saying it contradicted assurances given by federal officials during recent talks between the two sides."What was done today is truly surprising and in no way acceptable," Barzani told reporters in Erbil.He said Kurdish authorities had been given a different message during meetings with Iraqi federal representatives, who had assured them that outstanding disputes would be resolved through dialogue and within the framework of Iraq's constitution."There have been mixed messages. The delegations we have met have given us a different message that pointed towards resolving outstanding issues on the basis of the constitution," Barzani said.He maintained that his government would respect constitutional decisions but would not accept measures it considered unconstitutional. He also said preserving the Kurdistan region's constitutional status and protecting the interests of its people remained a priority.The reaction comes after Barzani met Zaidi in Baghdad on November 9 to discuss the region's share of the 2027 federal budget, oilfield management, revenue distribution and public-sector salaries. Both sides had agreed to work towards resolving their differences through constitutional means, according to the Kurdistan Regional Government.Why does Iraqi Kurdistan have control over its own affairsThe Kurdistan region has a high degree of self-government because of decades of conflict between Iraq's central government and its Kurdish population. Its autonomy, which began taking shape in the 1990s, was formally recognised under Iraq's 2005 constitution.The roots of Kurdish self-rule go back to the 1991 Gulf War. Following Iraq's defeat in the war, Kurdish groups in northern Iraq launched an uprising against then-president Saddam Hussein.Iraqi forces retaliated, forcing thousands of Kurdish families to flee their homes. The United States, Britain and France subsequently established a no-fly zone over northern Iraq to protect the Kurdish population from further attacks.Following the US-led invasion of Iraq in 2003 and the fall of Saddam Hussein, Kurdish leaders participated in the formation of the country's new political system. The 2005 Iraqi constitution formally recognised the Kurdistan region as a federal entity within Iraq under Article 117.Under Article 121, the regional government was granted executive, legislative and judicial powers in areas that do not fall exclusively under the federal government's authority. This allowed the Kurdistan Regional Government (KRG) to maintain its own parliament, presidency, ministries and internal security forces, known as the Peshmerga.The arrangement gives Erbil considerable authority over regional administration, security and economic affairs, while Baghdad retains control over key national responsibilities such as foreign policy, national defence, currency and customs policy.In 2017, the Kurdistan region also held an independence referendum, in which an overwhelming majority voted in favour of separation from Iraq.Baghdad rejected the vote, while neighbouring countries and international powers opposed Kurdish independence. The referendum did not lead to independence, and the region remains part of federal Iraq.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Israel's PR war hits a wall as Gaza backlash erodes US public support
articles.summary: Israel is pouring millions of dollars into winning American hearts and minds, but the battle appears to be slipping away from Benjamin Netanyahu.
articles.body: Israel is pouring millions of dollars into winning American hearts and minds, but the battle appears to be slipping away from Benjamin Netanyahu.Despite declaring the fight for public opinion the country's "eighth front" and ramping up its public relations spending, Israel is struggling to hold on to its traditional support base in the US as its war in Gaza fuels growing anger among American voters.According to an Al Jazeera report, Israel has sharply expanded its public diplomacy campaign in the US, increasing its budget to $730 million in March 2026.The campaign includes hiring American public relations firms, engaging social media influencers and organising visits to Israel for journalists, emerging political figures and community leaders.However, these efforts come amid growing signs that American public opinion is turning against Israel, raising questions about the effectiveness of Netanyahu's influence campaign.The shift is reflected in recent opinion polls, which point to declining support for Israel among Americans. A growing section of the US public, particularly younger voters, has become increasingly critical of Israel's military campaign in Gaza.The change is also being felt within traditionally pro-Israel constituencies, including sections of the Republican Party, raising concerns in Israel over the erosion of a support base that has long been central to its relationship with Washington.But what is driving this shift in American public opinion? The prolonged war in Gaza, mounting civilian casualties and widespread images of destruction have played a major role in shaping perceptions of Israel.The backlash has also extended beyond Gaza, with the US-Israel military campaign against Iran adding to criticism among Americans who question Washington's growing involvement in Middle Eastern conflicts and the costs of backing Israel.The growing discontent is particularly significant for Netanyahu because it is no longer confined to Democrats or traditionally pro-Palestinian groups.Younger Republicans and sections of the MAGA movement have also begun questioning Washington's close alignment with Israel. Critics argue that US foreign policy is increasingly being shaped by Israeli interests, while concerns over military spending, fuel prices and the cost of overseas conflicts have added to the debate over continued American support for Netanyahu's government.For Netanyahu, the challenge now goes beyond countering criticism of Israel's military campaign. It strikes at the foundations of a relationship that has traditionally enjoyed bipartisan support in Washington.While declining public approval does not immediately translate into a shift in US policy or military assistance, sustained opposition among American voters could eventually put pressure on lawmakers and future administrations to rethink their approach towards Israel.The battle for the 'eighth front', once seen as an effort to strengthen Israel's image, is increasingly exposing the limits of its influence over American public opinion.You use AI every day. articles.title: A San Diego family auto-repair site was earmarked for a partnership to build 60 apartments, but the project stalled and the partners fell out; an appeals court has allowed the owners' lawsuit to stay in court
articles.summary: A plan to replace a family-run auto-repair business in San Diego with a 60-unit apartment building ended in a legal dispute after the development stalled
articles.body: A plan to replace a family-run auto-repair business in San Diego with a 60-unit apartment building ended in a legal dispute after the development stalled and the partners disagreed over their responsibilities. The property-owning company wanted to pursue its claims in court, while the developer argued that the dispute had to be resolved through arbitration under their business agreement.In a November 23, 2026 ruling, available on Justia, the California Court of Appeal, Fourth Appellate District, Division One, upheld a lower court's decision allowing the lawsuit to proceed in court. The published opinion in E&N, Inc. v. Haas held that the operating agreement of the limited liability company required a transfer of real estate and was therefore subject to state rules governing arbitration clauses in property-conveyance contracts.How the auto-repair property became part of a development dealThe dispute centres on a commercial property at 4040 Park Boulevard in San Diego. Angie Huynh and her late husband, Tai Diep, owned it through their company, E&N, Inc., and operated a family-run automobile repair shop there. In July 2021, E&N entered into a joint venture with real estate developer Daniel Haas and two companies associated with him, Haas Development LLC and HD Capital Partners LLC. Their plan was to redevelop the site into a 60-unit apartment building with retail space on the ground floor.The partners formed a limited liability company called 4040 Park LLC to carry out the project. Haas Development became its manager, while E&N and HD Capital were its two members. HD Capital received an 88.89 per cent ownership interest, leaving E&N with 11.11 per cent. Under the operating agreement, E&N was required to contribute the property to the new company. The agreement valued the site at $3.15 million and required E&N to place an executed and notarised grant deed with a neutral escrow agent, to be released for recording once specified conditions were met.HD Capital, meanwhile, agreed to make financial contributions. These included $100,000 shortly after signing, $1.9 million when the construction lender funded its first draw and $150,000 when permanent financing closed. It was also required to contribute an additional amount anticipated to be approximately $8 million, in amounts and at times determined by the developer.Why the partners ended up in courtA dispute developed over the project's timeline and the parties' financial contributions. In July 2024, E&N filed a lawsuit in San Diego County Superior Court against Haas and the related companies. The complaint alleged that the developer misrepresented the project's development timeline and projected income, failed to take preliminary steps needed to begin construction and denied E&N access to the company's financial records.E&N brought several claims, including intentional and negligent misrepresentation, violations of state securities laws, negligence, breach of the duty of good faith and fair dealing, unjust enrichment and a request for an accounting. These were allegations in the lawsuit, not findings that the developer had committed wrongdoing.Haas sought to move the dispute out of court and into arbitration, relying on a clause in the operating agreement. The clause required the company and its members to arbitrate disputes arising from the agreement if they could not be resolved through nonbinding mediation. E&N opposed the request, arguing that the arbitration clause did not meet the requirements of California Code of Civil Procedure section 1298. The trial court agreed and denied the motion to compel arbitration.Why the appeals court refused to order arbitrationHaas challenged that decision, arguing that the operating agreement was primarily a business arrangement governing the company's management and ownership, rather than a contract to convey real estate. It also argued that federal law should override the state requirements. The appeals court rejected both arguments. It found that the agreement expressly required E&N to transfer ownership of the property to a separate legal entity, making it a contract to convey real estate or, at minimum, one that contemplated such a transfer.Section 1298 requires arbitration provisions in covered property-conveyance contracts to carry a clearly labelled heading, specified formatting and a notice explaining that agreeing to arbitration means giving up the right to have disputes decided in court. The parties did not dispute that the clause in their operating agreement failed to meet those requirements.The court also declined to consider Haas's federal securities-law argument because it had not identified the specific federal law on which it relied. Its separate argument under the Federal Arbitration Act was raised too late and had not been presented to the trial court.The appeals court therefore affirmed the order denying arbitration and awarded E&N its costs of the appeal. The ruling does not decide whether the developer is liable for the allegations or determine the financial outcome of the dispute. It means the owners' lawsuit can continue in court rather than being sent to arbitration.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Florida woman dies mysteriously on Antarctic cruise despite 'excellent health', A year later, parents sue the company as they are still waiting for tissue samples taken during the autopsy
articles.summary: A 44-year-old American woman died during a luxury Antarctic cruise just days after embarking on what was supposed to be a fresh start in her career.
articles.body: A 44-year-old American woman died during a luxury Antarctic cruise just days after embarking on what was supposed to be a fresh start in her career. Her parents are now suing the cruise company and its ship operator, alleging that delays in emergency medical assistance and the actions of the vessel's doctor contributed to her death.Kristen Elizabeth Nolan, who had worked at Walt Disney World for 11 years, had recently left her job to sell luxury travel packages for Panache Cruises. The company had sent her on an Antarctic expedition so she could experience the journey firsthand and advise prospective customers. However, what was meant to be a career-defining opportunity ended in tragedy when Nolan died after spending a night camping on a glacier off the western coast of the Antarctic Peninsula in November 2025.A year later, her parents, Vickie Lynn Patterson and Terry Nolan, have now filed a lawsuit against Panache Cruises and HX Expeditions, formerly known as Hurtigruten, which owns and operates the cruise ship MS Fridtjof Nansen. They have alleged negligence and are seeking answers about the circumstances surrounding their daughter's death, the Daily Mail reported.According to the complaint, Nolan had been declared in "excellent" physical health before the expedition. She died on November 14, 2025, after being found cold and unresponsive at the campsite.What happened on the night of the tragedy?Nolan had travelled from Orlando, Florida, on November 9, 2025, beginning her journey with a stop in Buenos Aires before heading to Ushuaia and Antarctica. She was excited about the opportunity and had written on Instagram: "Buenos Aires here I come and on to Ushuaia and Antarctica!!!!" On November 13, Nolan and other passengers boarded an inflatable boat from the MS Fridtjof Nansen and crossed Dorian Bay to reach Damoy Point, where they were scheduled to spend the night camping on the ice.The group reached the shore at around 8 pm, carried their equipment across the snow and dug shallow shelters, according to the lawsuit.The campers had allegedly been led to believe that expedition guides would monitor them throughout the night. However, the complaint claims both guides went to sleep along with the campers, leaving nobody on watch or conducting regular checks.At some point during the night, another camper reportedly woke up to use the bathroom and heard Nolan crying inside her shelter. The woman allegedly assumed Nolan was having a private moment and continued without alerting the guides.The next morning, at approximately 5.05 am, the group began preparing to leave when Nolan was discovered pulseless, cold and unresponsive, the complaint states.Doctor reached her 21 minutes after emergency alertThe guides contacted the ship's bridge, alerting the onboard doctor, Dr Jasna Sena Tankosic, and a nurse. An emergency was declared at 5.08 am. However, according to the lawsuit, the medical team did not leave the ship until 5.17 am and reached the shore at 5.22 am. Tankosic reportedly reached Nolan at approximately 5.26 am, 21 minutes after the guides first raised the alarm. By then, Nolan's skin was turning blue and her body was beginning to stiffen, according to the court filing.The doctor allegedly believed Nolan had suffered a heart attack and administered three doses of epinephrine, commonly known as adrenaline, within six minutes.Her parents' lawsuit argues that repeated intravenous doses of epinephrine could be toxic for someone experiencing hypothermia.The complaint further alleged that the doctor made no attempt to warm Nolan's body. The family argued that hypothermia can produce signs resembling death, even when a person may still be revived, and that warming should have been attempted.The lawsuit also questioned whether Tankosic was adequately qualified to serve as the expedition vessel's sole physician. The doctor reportedly maintained a social media profile highlighting her work in cosmetic procedures and nutritional science and runs a medical spa in Belgrade.After returning to the ship, Tankosic declared Nolan dead from natural causes, according to the complaint.Family waited six weeks for her body to returnThe circumstances surrounding the handling and return of Nolan's remains have added to her family's distress.When Argentine authorities took custody of her body, they reportedly declined to conduct an autopsy because the death had not been classified as suspicious. Her parents hired an Argentine attorney and spent six weeks obtaining a court order for an examination. The autopsy report did not identify any factors or medical conditions that explained her sudden death, according to the lawsuit.Nolan's body remained in an Argentine morgue for nearly two months before being returned to the United States. Her family's attorney, Neil Bayer alleged that the remains were not preserved properly and there was mold on the body when it reached Florida. The condition was reportedly so disturbing that the funeral director handling Nolan's arrangements refused to allow her mother to view her body.Family still waiting for belongings and medical samplesThe family alleged that several of Nolan's personal belongings went missing in the aftermath of her death. According to the complaint, her parents waited months for boxes containing items from her cabin to arrive. Some belongings are still missing, including her Apple Watch and cellphone. A pair of Ray-Ban Meta smart glasses was also reportedly replaced inside its charging case with an inexpensive imitation pair.Nearly a year after Nolan's death, her parents are still trying to bring tissue samples collected during the autopsy back to the United States for independent testing.You use AI every day. When two to three candidates are contesting for a single post, the situation needs to be viewed seriously,” he said.Kadam, who had earlier written to chief minister Mohan Charan Majhi seeking intervention in the Kotia dispute, said the issue should not be left to the district administration alone. “The state govt must demonstrate its presence in the disputed region through deployment of senior ministers,” he said.“All political parties are united on the Kotia issue. The state govt should take every possible step to ensure that people from the disputed villages do not participate in the Andhra Pradesh elections,” Kadam said.Koraput BJP district president Siba Muduli said the BJP govt was committed to protecting Odisha’s territorial integrity and the interests of people living in Kotia. “The govt will take all necessary administrative and security measures to ensure that no Andhra Pradesh official enters the area to conduct elections. We will also create awareness among people and urge them not to participate in the elections being conducted by Andhra Pradesh,” Muduli said.Andhra Pradesh has included 21 disputed villages of Kotia under five panchayats for the elections, with polling scheduled for Dec 2. The nomination process concluded on Monday, with 131 candidates filing papers for sarpanch and ward member posts.Kotia gram panchayat, under Pottangi block, comprises 28 villages, of which 21 are at the centre of a longstanding territorial dispute between Odisha and Andhra Pradesh. The dispute dates back to 1968, with both states staking claims to the villages.
